Investing.com -- The White House has named senior officials and outside advisers to a new AI task force led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the Wall Street Journal reported exclusively.
Track major AI and technology stocks with InvestingPro - now 50% off
The "Super Intelligence Force" will have 120 days to report on AI risks and opportunities and determine the federal government’s responsibilities. Its work could be extended or transferred to a government agency.
Clayton, who will effectively serve as President Donald Trump’s AI czar, said falling behind other countries could increase known and unidentified risks, particularly those posed by U.S. adversaries.
The task force will have three vice chairs. Emil Michael, undersecretary of war for Research and Engineering, will coordinate with AI companies, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor will work with critical infrastructure providers and other industry stakeholders.
Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson will oversee consumer interests and groups representing areas including children, privacy, freedom of speech, religious faith and freedom of association.
Members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and deputy chief of staff Richard Walters.
External participants include venture capitalist David Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who will advise on national security.
The task force plans to work with AI companies to identify risks rather than replace industry-led safeguards. It will review existing laws and potential congressional action, alongside government systems for handling warnings involving breaches, hacks and AI model jailbreaks.
Its formation follows a White House meeting where OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang were among industry leaders agreeing to voluntary principles covering model monitoring, independent reviews and board-level safety notifications.
The task force’s charter calls for the U.S. to remain at the forefront of AI development while protecting Americans and avoiding regulation that could restrict innovation and competition.

title: Australia’s Chalmers blames U.S.-Iran war for higher inflation, borrowing costs
full_text:
U.S. debt could reach 160% of GDP within decade, Scope warns
Investing.com -- Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the U.S.-Iran war has been an economic "disaster," blaming the conflict for higher inflation and borrowing costs and warning that it is weighing on global growth, Bloomberg reported.
"Whatever the reasons were for going in, from an economic point of view the war in the Middle East has been a disaster," Chalmers told ABC News’ Insiders program on Sunday.
Chalmers said higher costs stemming from the conflict were affecting Australians and consumers elsewhere, with upward pressure on inflation contributing to higher interest rates globally. Asked whether U.S. President Donald Trump should end the war, Chalmers declined to offer advice but said an end to the conflict "can’t come soon enough."
His comments come after Australia’s central bank raised interest rates to a 15-year high in an effort to curb inflation, citing elevated energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict alongside domestic capacity pressures.
Chalmers rejected suggestions that government spending was the primary driver of Australian inflation, saying spending growth had slowed.
The government is preparing a savings package for its mid-year budget update. Chalmers warned that rising global bond yields would add "some billions of dollars" to the government’s debt-servicing costs.
He said intensifying borrowing-cost pressures were affecting government budgets globally, with the final impact on Australia’s fiscal position still uncertain.
Chalmers said Australia was not anticipating a recession but warned that weaker global growth from the conflict would also affect the domestic economy.
Separately, Chalmers said he would travel to Japan on Sunday to meet Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, business leaders and investors.
The discussions will cover challenges including higher energy prices and bond yields, as well as efforts to increase investment, strengthen fuel security and improve economic resilience between Australia and Japan.

title: Apple to flag AI requests for Mac data after Meta’s Muse complaints
full_text:
U.S. debt could reach 160% of GDP within decade, Scope warns
Investing.com -- Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) said it plans to change its Mac operating system to make it clearer when artificial intelligence agents request access to all data stored on a computer, Reuters reported Friday.
The move follows complaints about Meta Platforms’ (NASDAQ:META) Muse AI agent, which can perform complex tasks such as cancelling unused subscriptions and negotiating lower prices. Some users claimed Muse accessed messages they believed were private.
Apple’s iPhones and iPads use sandboxing, which prevents individual apps from accessing data inside other apps by default. Macs offer greater flexibility through a "Full Disk Access" setting that allows applications such as cloud backup services to access all data on a machine with user permission.
Apple said some developers were using the feature in ways that could expose users to risks.
The company plans to introduce additional controls requiring users who want to give an application that level of access to take a more explicit action.
"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said.
The company said it wants users to understand the potential risks before granting applications access to their data.
Apple’s announcement follows claims by Inc magazine technology columnist Jason Aten that Muse read private messages stored on his Mac. Aten said he had not enabled Full Disk Access.
Meta spokesperson Andy Stone disputed the claims last week, saying access to Apple’s Messages app through Muse is strictly opt-in.
Stone said users must enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector before Muse can read Messages content. He added that users can revoke that permission at any time.
Apple declined to comment beyond its published statement. Meta did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
The changes put additional attention on operating-system permissions as increasingly autonomous AI agents gain the ability to perform tasks across applications and access information stored on users’ devices.

title: Reaction roundup: Experts, analysts weigh in on September jobs report
full_text:
U.S. debt could reach 160% of GDP within decade, Scope warns
Investing.com -- Wall Street’s focus on Friday was on the September nonfarm payrolls report which showed significantly weaker-than-expected job growth, prompting traders to pare their expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike later this month.
As per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, nonfarm payrolls rose 29k last month, significantly lower than the estimated figure of 89k. The monthly growth was the slowest of the year. Moreover, nonfarm employment in July and August combined were revised down by 60k. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.
The data comes at a time when separate indicators have suggested a resilient U.S. economy and a slight moderation in stubbornly high inflation. Any signs of labor market weakness in such a scenario means a central bank would typically hold interest rates steady, as tightening policy can quell price pressures but at the risk of further denting economic growth and labor activity.
The reaction in Fed October rate expectations reflected the same. As per the CME FedWatch tool, the odds of a quarter-point rate hike later this month fell to nearly 22% while those of the central bank holding rates steady surged to about 78%.
Wall Street and the U.S. Treasury bond market caught a bid after the jobs report. The enthusiasm faded slightly later in Friday’s session, with U.S. stocks paring some gains and yields rising again. The 10-year Treasury yield was last up 3.4 basis points to 5.272%.
Here are some popular exchange-traded funds that track the benchmark S&P 500 index: SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, and iShares Core S&P 500 ETF.
See below for various reactions to the jobs data:
Dan Alpert, executive chairman at Westwood Capital:
“This was a miss that will take pressure off the Fed and the bond market. Equities rallying on bad news = good news.”
Michael Feroli, chief U.S. economist at JPMorgan:
“Nonfarm employment increased only 29,000 last month, and the gains for the prior two months were revised down by a net 60,000. That left the 3-month average gain at 51,000 last month, which is close to most estimates of trend monthly growth in the labor supply, i.e. breakeven job growth.
Wage growth has been decelerating, a trend which continued last month as average hourly earnings were up only 0.1% for the month and 3.0% over a year ago. That deceleration should give comfort to Fed policymakers that the economy is not overheating in a way that calls for a hurried rate hike cycle.
It would now take a very strong CPI to make the October meeting live. We continue to look for another hike at the December FOMC meeting, on the assumption that the September and October price reports show still-sticky trends in core inflation.”
Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial:
“We are seeing the tension between the goods-producing sectors that support the AI boom and the services-producing sectors that are feeling the impact of technological change. Given the overall softness of the labor market, the likelihood of two Fed hikes is getting lower.”
Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial:
“There is zero chance for a rate hike in October now—in retrospect, September should have been a hold. Outside of energy, the inflation impulse is lower, and Fed was zigging when it should have been zagging.”
Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG U.S.:
“The Fed is (expected) to skip a rate hike in October and resume hikes in December. They are trying to prevent a larger blow to the labor market and engineer a softer landing. Still, the inflation data going into the October meeting will be ugly and hot due to the resurgence of energy prices. Elevated diesel prices could have a long tail, given the loss in global refining capacity due to the war in Ukraine and conflict in the Middle East.”
Joseph Brusuelas, principal and chief economist at RSM US:
“The low hire, low fire U.S. jobs market remains our baseline forecast and one should anticipate the soft pace of hiring to continue going forward. Statistically insignificant noise is the primary reason for the modest uptick in unemployment and full employment remains the best description of the American labor market currently.
The soft pace of hiring and noise around the size of the domestic labor force should support those at the Federal Reserve looking to keep the federal funds policy rate on hold at the upcoming October meeting. The September data implies little to no risk of second round wage induced inflation and the fact of the matter is that the Fed is simply not worried about the employment side of their mandate at the current time.
Our baseline call on the direction of monetary policy remains no hike in October and one twenty-five basis point hike in December and then another in March of 2027.”
Justin Wolfers, professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan:
“An all around weak -- but not tragic -- payrolls report for September.”

title: AI deal boom drives Hong Kong fundraising to record summer - Bloomberg
full_text:

Investing.com -- Hong Kong share sales raised a record $47.5 billion in the third quarter as Chinese technology companies tapped investors for capital to fund artificial intelligence expansion, Bloomberg reported.
Initial public offerings, placements and block trades during the July-to-September period produced the largest fundraising haul ever for those months, pushing the city’s total for 2026 above $92 billion. That puts Hong Kong within reach of the $112.5 billion annual record set in 2021.
Alibaba Group’s $10.2 billion follow-on offering was the quarter’s largest transaction. Zhongji Innolight raised almost $8 billion in Hong Kong’s biggest listing in nearly seven years.
AI model developer Z.AI has raised $9.6 billion this year through its IPO, placements and convertible bonds. MiniMax and chipmakers Shanghai Iluvatar CoreX Semiconductor and Shanghai Biren Technology also returned to investors shortly after their IPO lockups expired.
The activity reflects growing capital requirements among Chinese companies competing in AI and related technologies. Some businesses are returning to equity markets only months after earlier fundraising rounds.
The boom spread across Asia-Pacific, where third-quarter share sales exceeded $120 billion, the highest for the period in six years. India raised a record $26 billion since July, supported by domestic liquidity.
Investor appetite is becoming more selective as markets weaken. The MSCI Asia-Pacific Index fell as much as 7% in July amid questions about returns from heavy AI spending, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Tech Index has trended lower this year.
Only two of Hong Kong’s 10 largest deals since July are currently trading above their offer prices. Higher bond yields and expectations for further Federal Reserve rate increases are also tightening financial conditions.
The deal pipeline remains substantial, with additional offerings planned across the region, including major listings in India, the Philippines and Australia.

title: FlyDubai copilot lost earlier job over radical views
full_text:

Investing.com -- The FlyDubai copilot accused of attacking the captain of a Tel Aviv-bound flight previously worked for Oman Air before being dismissed over engagement with views considered radical, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the situation.
Hamam al-Hammami, 29, had previously been identified by Israeli authorities as an Omani citizen, but details of his identity, age and employment history had not been disclosed until this weekend.
UAE investigators said Saturday that the copilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act by attacking the captain with an ax kept in the cockpit for emergencies and trying to seize control of the aircraft.
Flight FZ1073, carrying more than 170 passengers, was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Sept. 30. Passengers and members of a reserve crew intervened to subdue al-Hammami and stabilise the aircraft before it landed safely at an airport in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi investigators have since said the two pilots were transferred to Abu Dhabi.
FlyDubai CEO Ghaith Al Ghaith previously said there were still "many questions" surrounding the incident and that the investigative process should be allowed to establish the facts.
The investigation is examining possible motives and whether other parties may have been connected to the incident, UAE federal prosecutor Hamad Al Shamsi said Saturday. Authorities are also conducting technical examinations of physical and digital evidence.
The presence of an Omani pilot aboard a flight bound for Israel has also drawn scrutiny because Oman and Israel do not have formal diplomatic relations.
Israeli Transportation Minister Miriam Regev called the situation a breach of existing arrangements and asked Israel’s Shin Bet security agency to investigate.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said several questions remain unanswered, including whether the copilot held another citizenship. He also said authorities were examining the possibility that the incident was intended to damage relations between Israel and the UAE.

title: Houthis claim strike on Saudi Aramco facility as Yemen fighting intensifies
full_text:

Investing.com -- Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked a major Saudi Aramco oil facility near Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, as fighting between the group and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces intensified.
Flames and a large plume of smoke rose from the Aramco refinery on Saturday, as firefighters responded to the blaze. Saudi authorities and Aramco had not immediately confirmed what caused the fire.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the attacks caused fires at the targeted sites and were retaliation for Saudi air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, including Sanaa. He said about 60 air attacks had been carried out over the previous 24 hours.
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces confirmed air strikes on Sanaa and Saada. Fighting also intensified around Taiz, where Houthis launched coordinated attacks against government positions along a roughly 15-kilometre front. Shelling killed a 14-day-old baby in a residential area of Dhubab, according to Al Jazeera.
Government-aligned forces separately claimed 97 attacks against Houthi positions in Taiz and Lahij, after reporting another 257 operations across several areas. Al Jazeera said it could not independently verify the military’s casualty claims.
Pressure on Iran also continued. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Washington’s blockade around the Strait of Hormuz remained "ironclad" and warned that President Donald Trump retained options if Tehran did not change course.
Iran’s rial, meanwhile, fell to a fresh low near 2.7 million per dollar on the free market. Iranian state television said the central bank had begun selling up to $2 billion to support the currency, which has lost more than half its value over the past year.
Russia also offered to mediate between Washington and Tehran. Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev said Moscow was prepared to help end the conflict and would not sacrifice its relationship with Iran.

Investing.com -- Bitcoin hovered near $85,000 on Sunday as investors weighed a new U.S. regulatory development that could expand leveraged exposure to the world’s largest cryptocurrency.
Bitcoin traded at $84,860.5 as of 01:29 ET (05:29 GMT), little changed over the past 24 hours. The token has remained in a relatively narrow range after briefly climbing above $87,000 earlier in the week.
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday approved a Cboe BZX rule change allowing the exchange to list six triple-leveraged exchange-traded products from Volatility Shares.
The products target three times the daily performance of bitcoin, ether, gold, silver, crude oil and natural gas. The bitcoin and ether products would provide leveraged exposure through futures rather than directly holding the cryptocurrencies.
The decision does not mean the products are immediately available for trading. Registration requirements must still be completed before shares can be publicly offered.
The development adds another potential route for investors seeking cryptocurrency exposure after the SEC separately proposed changes to crypto custody rules this week. That custody proposal was a major focus for Bitcoin markets on Friday.
Beyond regulation, signs of stronger industry activity are emerging. CryptoJobsList recorded 1,241 cryptocurrency job openings in September, up from 382 in July. Finance was the largest category, followed by engineering and trading, with Bitcoin the most frequently requested blockchain expertise.
Artificial intelligence could become another source of demand for blockchain infrastructure. ARK Invest CEO Cathie Wood said investors may increasingly need to "follow the agents" as AI systems move from answering questions to independently carrying out transactions.
Open blockchain networks and stablecoins are being considered as potential payment infrastructure for such systems. BlackRock has argued that AI agents could eventually pay autonomously for computing power, data and other digital services, creating potential demand for machine-to-machine payment networks.
Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong recently said Grok was the leading client for agentic traders on Coinbase, though he provided no figures.
Separately, Rich Dad Poor Dad author Robert Kiyosaki reiterated his support for Bitcoin as protection against monetary instability, comparing ownership of scarce assets with financial preparedness. His preferred assets also include gold, silver, and oil.

title: Japan PM protests to U.S. after Marine arrested over Okinawa murder
full_text:

Investing.com -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi lodged a protest with the United States on Sunday after a U.S. Marine was arrested on suspicion of robbing and murdering a Japanese woman in Okinawa.
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa prefecture, on Saturday and taking her wallet and backpack, Japanese police said. Ballard has denied the allegations.
Takaichi described the incident as "extremely brutal and vicious" and said the Japanese government had strongly protested to the U.S.
Tokyo is seeking maximum U.S. cooperation with the investigation, tighter discipline among American military personnel and measures aimed at preventing similar incidents.
The U.S. embassy and Marine Corps expressed condolences and said they were cooperating with Japanese authorities.
The Marine Corps confirmed that Ballard, who is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, remained in Japanese custody. It said it takes the allegations seriously and expects Marines to maintain high standards of conduct.
Okinawa hosts most of the roughly 18,000 U.S. Marines stationed in Japan. The American military presence has repeatedly generated opposition among some residents over aircraft noise, crashes and the conduct of personnel.
The arrest could add pressure to longstanding tensions surrounding U.S. bases in Okinawa. A 1995 rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three U.S. servicemen triggered widespread protests.
The latest incident could also complicate Takaichi’s efforts to relocate some Marines from the heavily populated Futenma air base to a facility at Henoko. Opponents of the plan have called for the troops to be moved outside Okinawa entirely.
Okinawa’s location near Taiwan gives the prefecture strategic importance for both Tokyo and Washington as they seek to deter potential Chinese military aggression in the region.

title: UK lawmakers warn reliance on U.S. cloud giants poses strategic risk - Bloomberg
full_text:
U.S. debt could reach 160% of GDP within decade, Scope warns
Investing.com -- Britain’s growing reliance on U.S. cloud providers for critical public services poses a "strategic and economic vulnerability," lawmakers warned, as concerns mount over Washington’s potential legal authority over data and services, Bloomberg reported.
UK government departments spend about £1 billion ($1.3 billion) annually on cloud services, according to parliamentary committee estimates. Amazon Web Services and Microsoft may account for as much as 80% of government cloud purchases, though officials do not know the precise level of dependence.
Chi Onwurah, chair of parliament’s science, innovation and technology committee, raised concerns over the U.S. CLOUD Act. Experts told the committee that U.S.-headquartered providers could be compelled to disclose data stored on their servers or withdraw services under certain circumstances.
The issue has gained urgency as health, defence, and tax services migrate to U.S.-owned cloud platforms.
HM Revenue & Customs awarded AWS a £473 million, 10-year contract to manage UK tax data in the past year. Britain’s defence ministry signed a £400 million agreement with Google Cloud, and National Health Service trusts are moving patient records from servers to U.S. cloud providers.
Government departments said their data was protected in UK-based data centres and contracts were subject to security and data protection requirements.
Onwurah said Britain was unlikely to build a domestic competitor capable of matching the largest U.S. providers and suggested greater cooperation with France and Germany.
European governments are already pursuing alternatives. France replaced Microsoft Azure with domestic provider Scaleway for its national health data hub in April, and Germany’s Schleswig-Holstein has shifted from Microsoft products towards open-source alternatives.
The European Commission is also developing a framework intended to increase Europe’s cloud and AI sovereignty.
The UK government said it was working to strengthen resilience and improve public-sector cloud procurement, with departments required to consider risks associated with excessive dependence on individual suppliers.

title: South Korea orders financial sector security checks after data breaches
full_text:

Investing.com -- South Korean regulators ordered financial institutions to carry out security inspections after a series of cyberattacks exposed personal information belonging to tens of thousands of customers.
Financial Services Commission Chairman Lee Eog-weon called for swift and thorough checks across the financial sector following an emergency meeting Sunday with executives from financial institutions and industry groups.
Institutions were instructed to complete internal inspections promptly and report their findings to authorities as regulators assess vulnerabilities exposed by the recent attacks.
Initial investigations indicate that some attackers targeted external websites and servers used by loan agents and employees, which received less security monitoring than core financial systems.
Lee said authorities could not rule out artificial intelligence being used in the attacks. He called for faster development of security systems capable of using AI to defend against AI-powered threats.
Several South Korean financial institutions have recently reported breaches. About 40,000 customers at Yegaram Savings Bank were affected, along with around 25,000 customers at Shinhan Bank.
KB Kookmin Bank, BNK Busan Bank and Hyundai Capital were also among the financial institutions affected by recent security incidents, according to Yonhap.
The breaches have increased pressure on banks and regulators to strengthen oversight of systems sitting outside institutions’ main technology infrastructure, including those accessed by third-party agents and employees.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung was briefed on the breaches and the government’s response, according to presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung.
Kang said the president viewed the incidents with "grave concern" and had instructed officials to conduct a thorough investigation and prepare measures in response.
The push comes as financial institutions face the prospect of increasingly sophisticated cyber threats, with regulators now examining whether AI tools played a role in the latest incidents.

By Branko filipovic
SARAJEVO/BANJA LUKA, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Bosnians vote on Sunday in elections that could affect their European Union membership bid and the influence that the United States and Russia seek over the small Balkan nation.
Voters are casting ballots for the country’s central tripartite presidency and national parliament, alongside regional legislative races in its two federal entities.
Voter frustration has grown over an economic slowdown, the slow pace of EU entry talks and a lingering political crisis in which the ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities have repeatedly stalled decisions by the weak central government that links them.
Bosnia, which has struggled to recover from the bloody 1992-95 war, secured EU candidate status in December 2022 and the green light to open accession negotiations in 2024. Actual talks have not started because domestic political leaders have yet to enact core requirements such as bolstering judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws.
Preliminary results are expected to be released by the Central Election Commission after polls close at 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) on Sunday.
The Bosnian war ended in 1995 with the US-brokered Dayton peace accord, which left the country split along ethnic lines into the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation — linked by the central government and tripartite presidency.
Many voters in the country of 3.4 million people say they want to move beyond the divisive rhetoric, but the politics appears stuck.
Dusan Cvijic, a 76-year-old pensioner from Banja Luka, the largest city of the Republika Srpska, said the government’s policies failed. “What has been done so far has been inadequate. People are struggling; life is very hard. There are ways to improve ..., if things are done honestly, to give people a decent life,” Cvijic said.
The vote pits rival ethnic parties — the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH — against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.
According to tracking platform Poliwave, the SDA holds a narrow national lead with 21.4%, followed by the SDP on 16.7%. In Republika Srpska, SNSD, the party run by secessionist leader Milorad Dodik, who wants close ties with Serbia and Russia, is ahead with 34.2%.
If ethnically based parties prevail and continue their bickering within the central government, which would be the body that would eventually officially join the EU, progress on accession is likely to be stalled further.
In the capital, Sarajevo, Ismar Garasljevic, a 51-year-old high school teacher, said: "More than 30 years after the war, the situation is still the same; we are talking about nationalism ... The same faces, the same story, constantly."
Voters on Sunday will face redesigned ballots alongside new biometric voter identification and electronic scanners introduced to curb voting fraud.
US AND RUSSIAN INFLUENCE
Major powers have long sought influence over Bosnia. The EU is seeking to expand its membership across the Balkans, including Bosnia, but Russia is slowing it down, maintaining its support of the Republika Srpska.
The US has also sought to gain influence and wants to push for a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US liquefied natural gas, run by a company with links to the Trump administration, but the EU warned that the company selection lacked competitive transparency.
Washington has also clashed with Brussels over the role of the international High Representative, who, under provisions of the Dayton accord, enforces the laws. Christian Schmidt, a former German government minister, resigned in May under pressure from the US.

title: Germany’s Merz arrives in Kyiv with €1.35bn aid package, drone deal in focus
full_text:
U.S. debt could reach 160% of GDP within decade, Scope warns
Investing.com -- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday with new military and energy assistance, as Germany and Ukraine prepare to finalise an agreement to jointly produce drones and other weapons.
Merz is expected to announce the release of €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for repairs to Ukraine’s energy sector, German government officials said.
The visit comes amid escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Merz said Ukraine would need continued support in the coming weeks and pledged to reassure President Volodymyr Zelenskiy of Germany’s commitment.
The chancellor travelled with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a business delegation including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence and Quantum Systems.
A major focus is an expected agreement covering joint production of drones, missiles and related software. Zelenskiy said earlier this week that the two countries were close to finalising the arrangement.
The cooperation is expected to include rapid production of anti-jet drones. Quantum Systems has successfully tested the technology as Ukraine seeks additional ways to counter high-speed Russian attack drones.
Quantum and Ukrainian manufacturer WIY Drones formed a joint venture in April to produce the Strila interceptor drone and related air-defence technology.
The broader agreement also involves development and production of weapons with ranges exceeding 1,000 kilometres, giving Ukraine additional capabilities to strike targets inside Russia.
German officials said increased cooperation could direct technology and investment back into Germany’s defence industry and strengthen protection against drone threats to critical infrastructure.
Merz is also expected to press Kyiv for progress on reforms requested by European Union partners, including efforts to combat corruption.
Russia said Saturday it would continue striking targets in Ukraine, describing the attacks as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory. Zelenskiy separately said Ukrainian forces would intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s strikes on civilian infrastructure.

title: Citi explains why home improvement stocks are lagging in 2026
full_text:
U.S. debt could reach 160% of GDP within decade, Scope warns
Investing.com -- Uncertainty around interest rates, energy costs, housing affordability, and geopolitics is weighing on the U.S. home improvement industry and its stocks in 2026, Citi analysts said after attending the HIRI Home Improvement Insights Summit.
Economists participating in the summit broadly expect home improvement demand to remain flat over the next 12 months. Higher rates and weak housing affordability remain key constraints, offset partly by resilient consumers, a stable jobs market and household wealth.
Mortgage rates remain a major hurdle. HIRI survey data indicated that rates in the 5% range could be an important psychological threshold for homeowners considering moving from existing mortgages. About 80% of homeowners with mortgages currently have rates below 6%, and half have rates below 4%.
Project delays are also weighing on demand. A homeowner survey found roughly one-third of projects are currently being delayed or cancelled. A separate contractor survey showed 60% of professionals had experienced at least one cancelled project, a substantial increase from last year.
Economic conditions and inflation were frequently cited as reasons. Projects proceeding are increasingly focused on maintenance and repairs, with some also being scaled down to meet tighter budgets.
Longer-term industry fundamentals remain supportive. Americans now remain in their homes for an average of 10 to 11 years, compared with roughly seven to eight years previously. The average U.S. housing stock is 44 years old, creating growing maintenance requirements.
Homeowners also hold about $450,000 in average household equity, providing a potential source of spending capacity. The U.S. has experienced roughly two decades of underbuilding in single-family homes, according to an economist from the National Association of Home Builders.
Artificial intelligence could reduce friction for retailers and contractors. Lowe’s technology chief said its strategy centres on augmenting employees rather than replacing them, with potential efficiency gains also available in contractors’ back-office operations.
Recent weakness in home improvement stocks suggests investors are pricing in the possibility that sluggish industry growth extends into 2027.
